sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Gastric Hypomotility Unmasking a Phytobezoar After Cryoballoon Pulmonary Vein Isolation》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Body · section-1-p1】Epigastric or chest pain in the first hours after left atrial ablation is a diagnostic trap: it can equally signal a lethal vascular or esophageal complication or a benign, self‐limiting one. Gastric hypomotility from periesophageal vagal injury is an established, if uncommon, extracardiac effect of ablation [1, 2]; its association with a gastric phytobezoar is unusual. We describe a patient in whom cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) was followed by two sequential diagnostic pivots—marked gastric dilatation and then a phytobezoar.

【Body · section-1-p7】Periesophageal vagal branches governing gastric and pyloric function lie millimeters from the ablation target, and cryoballoon technology reduces but does not abolish this proximity. In this patient the left‐sided veins—nearest the esophagus—received the coldest and longest applications, a pattern that fits periesophageal neural involvement without proving it. That luminal esophageal temperature remained within the safety range does not argue against this mechanism: luminal thermometry samples the esophageal lumen rather than the vagal fibers coursing on its anterior surface, and periesophageal vagal injury is described despite unremarkable luminal readings [2]. That such injury underlies post‐ablation gastric hypomotility is established [1, 2], and symptomatic hypomotility after cryoballoon ablation is reported [5]. We claim no new mechanism.

We describe a patient in whom cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) was followed by two sequential diagnostic pivots—marked gastric dilatation and then a phytobezoar.

Periesophageal vagal branches governing gastric and pyloric function lie millimeters from the ablation target, and cryoballoon technology reduces but does not abolish this proximity. That luminal esophageal temperature remained within the safety range does not argue against this mechanism: luminal thermometry samples the esophageal lumen rather than the vagal fibers coursing on its anterior surface, and periesophageal vagal injury is described despite unremarkable luminal readings [2]. That such injury underlies post‐ablation gastric hypomotility is established [1, 2], and symptomatic hypomotility after cryoballoon ablation is reported [5]. We claim no new mechanism.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Gastric Hypomotility Unmasking a Phytobezoar After Cryoballoon Pulmonary Vein Isolation》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Body · section-1-p2】A 62‐year‐old woman (body mass index 26.9 kg/m2) with EHRA class II atrial fibrillation refractory to propafenone underwent cryoballoon PVI. She had no diabetes, prior gastric or bariatric surgery, autonomic neuropathy, or psychiatric illness. She had received a proton pump inhibitor in 2021–2023 and again after rivaroxaban was started. Two upper gastrointestinal endoscopies in 2021 showed antral gastritis without a bezoar; no interval abdominal cross‐sectional imaging or repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was available before ablation. Pulmonary vein isolation was achieved and sinus rhythm restored (82 bpm); nadir balloon temperatures were −45°C and −49°C (240 s each) for the left‐sided pulmonary veins and −40°C and −43°C (180 s each) for the right‐sided veins. Luminal esophageal temperature was monitored throughout and stayed within the routine safety range, without triggering cryoenergy interruption. She was discharged asymptomatic.

evidence.text: A 62‐year‐old woman (body mass index 26.9 kg/m2) with EHRA class II atrial fibrillation refractory to propafenone underwent cryoballoon PVI. She had no diabetes, prior gastric or bariatric surgery, autonomic neuropathy, or psychiatric illness. She had received a proton pump inhibitor in 2021–2023 and again after rivaroxaban was started. Two upper gastrointestinal endoscopies in 2021 showed antral gastritis without a bezoar; no interval abdominal cross‐sectional imaging or repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was available before ablation. Pulmonary vein isolation was achieved and sinus rhythm restored (82 bpm); nadir balloon temperatures were −45°C and −49°C (240 s each) for the left‐sided pulmonary veins and −40°C and −43°C (180 s each) for the right‐sided veins. Luminal esophageal temperature was monitored throughout and stayed within the routine safety range, without triggering cryoenergy interruption. She was discharged asymptomatic.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:

【FIGURE 1 · joa370512-fig-0001】FIGURE 1 Chest radiographs before (A) and 24 h after (B) cryoballoon ablation, showing an interval increase in the gastric air–fluid level and distension.

【FIGURE 2 · joa370512-fig-0002】FIGURE 2 Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (coronal). (A) Marked gastric dilatation, with the magnified region indicated. (B) Magnified view of the gastric lumen showing a mottled intragastric mass with entrapped gas (dashed outline and arrows)—the characteristic appearance of a bezoar—present one week before endoscopy and attributed at the time to retained food.

【FIGURE 3 · joa370512-fig-0003】FIGURE 3 Initial upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (A, B): Large phytobezoar with vegetable‐fiber content (arrows); no pyloric stenosis, mucosal injury, or obstruction.
